Part 4 reads the chart that the class built, treats the idea of a multiverse at length, and closes on the analysis that you preregister before running it. The part takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The multiverse

**On the slides.** The slides name what you did in Task 4, your own small multiverse, and say where the idea comes from, with the garden of forking paths drawn. The slides go on to the filters for inclusion, enumeration against curation and the purposes that a multiverse can serve, and end on decomposing the variance by decision and on reading a specification curve.

To go further: [The multiverse and its critics](../../companion/multiverse.qmd).

## 2. The class chart and the curve

**On the slides**, with the Multiverse page open in another tab.

[Open the Multiverse page](../../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

The exploratory dots of the class are set against the curve of 864. You place a bet in the chat on which decision moves the estimates most, before the slides show the decomposition. The slides then place the five reanalyses and the original study on the curve, and show what the options off the curve do to it.

## 3. Your placement

[Open the browser lab at Task 4](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-4-explore){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Rerun the specification that you submitted with `try_spec()`, read off your own placement among the 864 specifications of the curve, and send it in the chat when the facilitator says go. Without a submission of your own, use the placement of the reproduced specification, which is 67%.

## 4. Reading a specification curve

**On the slides**, with the page on reading a specification curve open in another tab.

[Open Reading a specification curve](../../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

The slides say what the curve leaves out, and separate the two jobs that a curve can do, description and inference. The slides show why the 864 estimates depend on one another and are not 864 tests, how a permutation design builds the distribution against which a curve-level test is read, and what stands without the test. A discussion follows.

## 5. Critics and preregistration

**On the slides.** The slides present the three critical positions on multiverse analysis and the argument that a fully specified question has one correct analysis, with the question of how anyone would identify it. The slides end on what preregistration settles and what it leaves open, and set the exploration of Task 4 against the declaration of Task 5.

## 6. Task 5 – The preregistration

[Open the browser lab at Task 5](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-5-my-preregistration){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

If you work in the workspace, use the preregistration block in your report instead. Complete the block before you run anything, run `prereg()`, and type "declared" in the chat. When the class has declared, go on to [build, run and report](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-5-build-run-report). Translate the declaration into model syntax yourself, run it, and submit it with `report_result()`. Your result is drawn on the chart as a declared one beside the exploratory round.

## 7. The close

**On the slides**, with the [class chart](../../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd#class-results) on screen. The day closes on two points from the literature, the single analytical path, what you take with you, and the feedback form.

**By the end of the part** you have your own placement among the 864 specifications of the curve, one specification fixed in a preregistration before it was run, and its result on the class chart, together with an answer to what the curve that you joined does and does not establish.
